content: 1. The responsibility for ensuring successful tuberculosis treatment lies with the public health program or private healthcare provider, not the patient. 2. It is strongly recommended that the initial treatment strategy incorporates patient-centered case management, including an adherence plan that emphasizes directly observed therapy (DOT). 3. Treatment regimens are rated based on the strength of evidence supporting their use, and where applicable, other interventions are also rated. 4. Sputum cultures should be obtained at the end of the initial treatment phase to identify patients at increased risk of relapse. 5. Extended treatment is recommended for patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis who exhibit cavitation on the initial chest radiograph and have positive sputum cultures after two months of treatment. 6. The roles of rifabutin, rifapentine, and fluoroquinolones are discussed, including a regimen with once-weekly rifapentine during the continuation phase for selected patients. 7. Practical aspects of therapy, such as drug administration, use of fixed-dose combination preparations, monitoring and management of adverse effects, and drug interactions, are addressed. 8. Treatment completion is defined by the number of doses ingested and the duration of treatment administration. 9. Special treatment situations, including tuberculosis in children, HIV co-infection, extrapulmonary tuberculosis, culture-negative tuberculosis, pregnancy, breastfeeding, hepatic disease, and renal disease, are discussed in detail. 10. Updated recommendations are provided for managing tuberculosis caused by drug-resistant organisms. 11. These recommendations are compared with those of the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD), and the DOTS strategy is described. 12. The current status of research aimed at improving tuberculosis treatment is reviewed. 13. The primary goals of tuberculosis treatment are to cure the individual patient and to minimize the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to others. 14. Successful treatment benefits both the individual and the community, emphasizing the public health function of prescribing physicians. 15. Physicians are responsible not only for prescribing an appropriate regimen but also for ensuring the successful completion of therapy. 16. Treatment of tuberculosis is most effective within a comprehensive framework that addresses both clinical and social issues relevant to the patient. 17. Treatment should be tailored and supervised based on each patient’s clinical and social circumstances, following a patient-centered care approach. 18. Regardless of whether patients are managed in the private sector, by public health departments, or jointly, the health department is ultimately responsible for ensuring adequate diagnostic and treatment services and monitoring therapy outcomes. 19. Directly observed therapy (DOT), where patients are observed ingesting each dose of medication, is strongly recommended to maximize treatment adherence and completion. 20. Programs utilizing DOT as part of a comprehensive, patient-centered approach to case management have higher treatment completion rates than less intensive strategies. 21. 22. Recommended treatment regimens are largely based on evidence from clinical trials and are rated using a system developed by the United States Public Health Service (USPHS) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA). 23. There are four recommended regimens for treating patients with drug-susceptible tuberculosis, with modifications specified for certain circumstances. 24. The initial phase of treatment typically lasts two months, followed by a continuation phase of either four or seven months, depending on the patient’s clinical response and risk factors. 25. For most adult patients with previously untreated tuberculosis, the initial phase should include isoniazid (INH), rifampin (RIF), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB). 26. Ethambutol may be excluded once drug susceptibility results confirm that the organism is fully susceptible to isoniazid and rifampin. 27. For children whose visual acuity cannot be monitored, ethambutol is generally not recommended unless there is a high likelihood of isoniazid-resistant disease. 28. If pyrazinamide cannot be included in the initial phase due to contraindications (e.g., severe liver disease, gout, or pregnancy), the regimen should consist of isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol given daily for two months. 29. The continuation phase of treatment is typically four months for most patients but may be extended to seven months for those with cavitation on the initial chest radiograph and positive cultures at two months. 30. Patients with HIV infection and CD4+ cell counts below 100 cells/µL should receive daily or three-times-weekly therapy, as twice-weekly regimens are not recommended due to an increased risk of treatment failure or relapse. 31. Baseline evaluations for all patients should include sputum collection for microscopy and culture, chest radiography, and susceptibility testing for first-line drugs. 32. 33. Patients should be instructed to seek medical care promptly if symptoms recur after completing therapy. 34. Routine laboratory monitoring during treatment is not necessary unless baseline abnormalities or risk factors for hepatotoxicity are present. 35. For patients taking ethambutol, monthly assessments for visual disturbances are recommended, particularly for those receiving higher doses or prolonged therapy. 36. Patients at increased risk of treatment failure or relapse, such as those with cavitation on chest radiographs and positive cultures at two months, should undergo close microbiological monitoring. 37. The decision to initiate combination antituberculosis chemotherapy should be based on clinical, radiographic, and microbiological findings, as well as epidemiological considerations. 38. If tuberculosis is strongly suspected or the patient is seriously ill, treatment should be initiated promptly, even before microbiological confirmation. 39. For patients with culture-negative pulmonary tuberculosis, a diagnosis can be inferred based on clinical and radiographic improvement after two months of therapy. 40. Patients with latent tuberculosis infection may be treated with one of three regimens: isoniazid for nine months, rifampin with or without isoniazid for four months, or rifampin and pyrazinamide for two months. 41. Patients with HIV infection should undergo counseling and testing for HIV, and those with risk factors for hepatitis B or C should have serologic testing for these viruses. 42. Monthly sputum specimens should be obtained during treatment until two consecutive cultures are negative. 43. For patients with extrapulmonary tuberculosis, the frequency and type of evaluations depend on the site of disease. 44. Patients generally do not require follow-up after completing therapy but should be instructed to report any recurrence of symptoms.
